detail.longDescription:
by Kurtis Van Gent, Google Cloud, and Daryl Ducharme, Google Open Source Programs Office

Building production AI agents requires more than a capable reasoning model. Agents need a reliable way to connect to external systems and data, and they need procedural domain knowledge so they know how to use those tools safely without exhausting their context window.

Over the past year, open source communities have rallied around two complementary open standards to solve these challenges: the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for connecting agents to live tools, and Agent Skills for loading procedural instructions and scripts on demand. Following Anthropic's donation of the Agent Skills specification to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) alongside MCP, engineers from Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, and the wider ecosystem are now co-maintaining the standard under vendor-neutral governance.

To explore how open standards prevent ecosystem fragmentation, and why the best solutions don't always have to be homegrown, we sat down with Kurtis Van Gent, co-creator of the open source MCP Toolbox for Databases and a core maintainer on both MCP and Agent Skills.

From the N-by-M database problem to open source collaboration

Daryl Ducharme: How did your work on AI ecosystems for Google Cloud Databases and co-creating the open source MCP Toolbox for Databases lead to your role as a core maintainer on both the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent Skills?

Kurtis Van Gent: When I started my current role around three years ago, it was early in the generative AI cycle. My mission was to make it easy for developers to use cloud databases for their AI applications. As a strong proponent of developer experience, I loved that charter. As model reasoning improved, context and data were clearly the keys to making effective use of it, and there's no better place to store data than a database.

At the time, most database conversations focused on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) using vector search. However, our team believed that agents and tools held the most interesting potential for large language models (LLMs) going forward. We immediately hit two scaling challenges: Google Cloud supports more than 15 different databases across its portfolio, and new open source agent frameworks (starting with LangChain and LlamaIndex) were emerging every week.

That created a classic N-by-M integration problem between many clients and many data hosts. To solve it, we started GenAI Toolbox for Databases (now MCP Toolbox for Databases) as an open source framework for building and serving tools. We built our own server, clients, and protocol to standardize how agents look up and invoke database tools. Back then, agent terminology wasn't common vernacular yet, so every talk I gave had to start with three to five slides explaining what agents and tools actually were.

When Anthropic announced MCP, it was exciting validation that the broader ecosystem was arriving at the same architectural conclusions we were seeing across our database integrations. Rather than insisting on a homegrown protocol or spinning off a competing specification, we reached out to the MCP co-creators, Justin Spahr-Summers and David Soria Parra, and began meeting regularly. Because I believe strongly in open source communities and shared standards, I advocated for adopting MCP directly. We evolved our project into MCP Toolbox for Databases so it worked out of the box with any MCP client, and I focused on contributing capabilities from our original protocol back into the upstream MCP specification.

Leading the transition to a stateless MCP specification

Kurtis Van Gent: One of my primary upstream focuses was transport scalability. I began leading the MCP Transports Working Group with the goal of evolving the specification toward a stateless, horizontally scalable architecture. At first, it wasn't a crowded room. Our early working group meetings had around five participants, three of whom were from Google.

As MCP adoption accelerated across the industry, however, it became clear that early stateful assumptions around persistent sessions and initialization were holding MCP back at production scale. That effort culminated in a two-day Transports Summit where Google and fellow working group members hosted the MCP core maintainers at our San Francisco offices to work through the scaling bottlenecks and align on a path forward. Shortly afterward, I was invited to become an MCP core maintainer, both in recognition of our work identifying those transport challenges and to keep the Transports Working Group closely aligned with the core specification. The result of that collaboration was the July 28, 2026 MCP specification, which transitioned MCP to a stateless model.

That experience as an MCP core maintainer naturally positioned me to help co-maintain Agent Skills. Having already built working relationships with contributors across Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, stepping in to help steward Agent Skills inside the AAIF felt like a natural continuation of the same collaborative model.

Why vendor-neutral governance in the AAIF matters for developers

Daryl Ducharme: From your perspective as a core maintainer representing Google, why does bringing Agent Skills into the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) alongside MCP matter for developers and open source communities?

Kurtis Van Gent: We've seen open source technologies like Kubernetes achieve widespread adoption and sustained cross-company contributions, but organizations are understandably hesitant to build critical workflows on a specification controlled by a single vendor. Just as the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) provided a vendor-neutral home for container orchestration, the AAIF provides a neutral forum where organizations and independent maintainers can collaborate on shared agent standards.

Bringing Agent Skills into the AAIF signals how foundational this format has become across the AI ecosystem. Following in the footsteps of MCP, the organizations and open source communities adopting Agent Skills now have a shared seat at the table to shape how the specification evolves. For developers, this means you can author a skill once and trust that it will remain portable across different agents, IDEs, and harnesses without vendor lock-in.

Solving tool bloat with progressive disclosure: how MCP and Agent Skills fit together

Daryl Ducharme: You have spoken about the tension between "tool bloat" and context saturation when building production agents. How should developers think about the division of labor between MCP (connecting agents to live tools and data) and Agent Skills (loading procedural domain knowledge on demand)?

Kurtis Van Gent: One of the most impactful things MCP accomplished was commoditizing tools: it became straightforward for anyone to wrap a set of actions in an MCP server and share them. The unintended consequence was tool and context bloat. As agents grew more capable and connected to dozens of MCP servers, deciding which tool schemas and operational instructions to load into the context window became a major bottleneck.

Agent Skills introduced a remarkably simple, effective pattern for solving that problem through progressive disclosure. By loading only a lightweight YAML frontmatter name and description at startup, and pulling the full SKILL.md instructions, reference files, or scripts into context only when a task requires them, Agent Skills commoditized context the same way MCP commoditized tools.

While some observers initially viewed MCP and Agent Skills as competing approaches, they have always been complementary: Agent Skills package domain expertise into modular chunks that teach an agent how to approach a problem, while MCP provides the live execution interface to carry it out. Today, the broader ecosystem has converged on combining them, including efforts around Agent Plugins and proposals for serving Agent Skills over MCP so platform maintainers can distribute domain instructions and live tools together.

Putting MCP and Agent Skills to work in database and developer workflows

Daryl Ducharme: What is a concrete example of how developers are using Agent Skills and MCP together today—whether in Antigravity, database workflows, or across the broader ecosystem?

Kurtis Van Gent: Both MCP and Agent Skills have become ubiquitous across everyday developer workflows. In my own daily work, I write custom skills whenever I notice an agent struggling to get a repeatable workflow right on the first try. For example, I write skills for how I like to structure GitHub repositories or format commit messages so I never have to re-explain those conventions in a prompt.

At the platform level, our Google Cloud Databases team pairs MCP and Agent Skills together inside our Agent Plugins. When a developer using Antigravity connects to a PostgreSQL database on Cloud SQL or AlloyDB, they can install the corresponding Cloud SQL or AlloyDB plugin. From MCP, the agent gets a list of safe actions it can take against the database. From the bundled Agent Skills, it gets step-by-step instructions on how to use those tools for specific tasks, like provisioning an instance or configuring Identity and Access Management (IAM) database authentication securely—and because both specifications are open standards, the same SKILL.md and MCP pattern works across any open source database or agent harness.

That combination is both faster and safer than pointing an agent at raw documentation written for human readers. In our agent workflow benchmarks, we see developers complete complex database tasks much more quickly and reliably when MCP tools are paired with targeted Agent Skills.

What comes next for the Agent Skills specification

Daryl Ducharme: Working alongside maintainers from Anthropic, OpenAI, and the wider community inside the AAIF, what technical or governance areas are you most focused on next?

Kurtis Van Gent: Two major areas I'm focused on evolving next are packaging and discovery. Today, the Agent Skills specification defines how an individual skill is structured, but it doesn't yet standardize how collections of skills are bundled, how harnesses discover them, or how to resolve naming conflicts across skill sets. Closing those gaps will help address conformance differences across harnesses.

Versioning is another priority. As the Agent Skills specification matures under the AAIF, we need a clear, portable way for skill authors and agent harnesses to declare which version of the specification they support. I'm looking forward to working with the other maintainers and open source communities to standardize packaging, discovery, and versioning in upcoming releases.

How to get involved

Daryl Ducharme: For open source developers and maintainers who want to author portable skills or contribute to the specification and tooling at github.com/agentskills, where should they start?

Kurtis Van Gent: If you want to start authoring portable skills today, the documentation at agentskills.io walks through creating your first SKILL.md package in just a few minutes, and you can explore Google's open source catalog of developer skills at github.com/google/skills (along with our engineering retrospective on how we ship Google Agent Skills like products).

If you want to help shape the specification itself, visit the GitHub organization at github.com/agentskills to review open pull requests, file issues, and join the community Discord server where maintainers and contributors discuss upcoming specification proposals.
